items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The origin of life from non-living matter through natural chemical processes"?
items.answer: abiogenesis
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of abiogenesis.

items.stem: "The Miller–Urey experiment created living cells from gases." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It produced only simple organic molecules such as amino acids, not polymers or cells.
items.markingKey: It produced only simple organic molecules such as amino acids, not polymers or cells. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the main stages that must have occurred for the first cells to arise from non-living material.
items.answer: Synthesis of simple organic molecules (e.g. amino acids, nucleotides) from inorganic compounds; assembly into polymers; development of self-replicating molecules (e.g. RNA) to allow inheritance; enclosure of these molecules in membranes to form compartments (protocells) with a separate internal chemistry.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Synthesis of simple organic molecules (e.g. amino acids, nucleotides) from inorganic compounds; assembly into polymers; development of self-replicating molecules (e.g. RNA) to allow inheritance; enclosure of these molecules in membranes to form compartments (protocells) with a separate internal chemistry. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Chloé measured six guard cells using an eyepiece graticule with the × 40 objective lens. A stage micrometer showed that at this magnification one eyepiece unit (epu) = 2.5 µm.

Cell | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6
Length / epu | 17 | 16 | 14 | 15 | 19 | 12

(a) Calculate the actual length of cell 1 in µm. [1]
(b) Calculate the mean length of the six cells. [2]
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 17 × 2.5 = 42.5 µm (A1). (b) [2] Converts each to µm or mean epu × 2.5 (M1); 38.8 µm (A1).

items.stem: A protocell model consists of fatty-acid vesicles containing short RNA strands. Which property of life is it least able to show?
options: growth by taking up fatty acids
metabolism using enzymes made by the protocell
items.answer: metabolism using enzymes made by the protocell
items.markingKey: B. Such models lack a metabolic network.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The origin of the first cells can be explained by testable scientific hypotheses."
items.answer: Each stage is supported by experiments, but the whole process remains a hypothesis supported by indirect evidence; it is scientifically testable in parts but not fully explained.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: individual stages such as monomer synthesis (Miller–Urey) and vesicle formation have been reproduced in laboratories; ribozymes and genomic reconstruction of LUCA provide indirect evidence. Arguments against: the actual conditions of early Earth cannot be observed directly; no experiment has produced a living cell from non-living matter. Supported judgement: Each stage is supported by experiments, but the whole process remains a hypothesis supported by indirect evidence; it is scientifically testable in parts but not fully explained.

items.stem: Define the term "RNA world hypothesis".
items.answer: The hypothesis that early life used RNA both to store genetic information and to catalyse reactions, before DNA and proteins
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the hypothesis that early life used RNA both to store genetic information and to catalyse reactions, before DNA and proteins. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Why could cells not have arisen by spontaneous generation in today’s conditions?
options: Existing organisms would consume organic molecules, and free oxygen would oxidise them.
Organic molecules can no longer be formed.
items.answer: Existing organisms would consume organic molecules, and free oxygen would oxidise them.
items.markingKey: B. Pasteur showed cells arise from pre-existing cells today.

items.stem: Briefly describe the discovery of ribozymes by Thomas Cech and Sidney Altman and explain what it reveals about the RNA world hypothesis.
items.answer: Some RNA molecules were found to catalyse their own cutting and joining reactions. It showed that RNA can act as an enzyme as well as store information, so RNA could have been self-replicating.
items.markingKey: Context (Some RNA molecules were found to catalyse their own cutting and joining reactions.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It showed that RNA can act as an enzyme as well as store information, so RNA could have been self-replicating. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the RNA world hypothesis.

items.stem: Define the term "resolution".
items.answer: The ability to distinguish two points that are close together as separate; the minimum distance at which they can be seen as separate
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the ability to distinguish two points that are close together as separate; the minimum distance at which they can be seen as separate. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: "A higher magnification always shows more detail." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Detail depends on resolution; beyond the resolving limit, more magnification only enlarges a blurred image.
items.markingKey: Detail depends on resolution; beyond the resolving limit, more magnification only enlarges a blurred image. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the resolution of an electron microscope is greater than that of a light microscope.
items.answer: Resolution is limited by the wavelength of the radiation used; electron beams have a wavelength far shorter than visible light, so points much closer together (down to about 0.1–1 nm) can be distinguished. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Resolution is limited by the wavelength of the radiation used; electron beams have a wavelength far shorter than visible light, so points much closer together (down to about 0.1–1 nm) can be distinguished. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: The image of a palisade mesophyll cell in a micrograph at × 1000 is 42 mm long. What is its actual length?

Using the use of cryogenic electron microscopy to determine the structure of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein in 2020 as an example, explain how developments in microscopy improve biological understanding.
items.answer: Within weeks, cryo-EM revealed the spike protein’s shape at near-atomic resolution. Rapid freezing preserves the native structure and the short electron wavelength gives very high resolution, supporting vaccine design.
items.markingKey: Context (Within weeks, cryo-EM revealed the spike protein’s shape at near-atomic resolution.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Rapid freezing preserves the native structure and the short electron wavelength gives very high resolution, supporting vaccine design. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how developments in microscopy improve biological understanding.

items.stem: A scale bar 20 mm long on a micrograph represents 5 µm. What is the magnification?
Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Cell theory is a universal principle with no significant exceptions."
items.answer: Cell theory is robust as a general theory; apparent exceptions refine rather than overturn it, showing that scientific theories are generalisations that accommodate atypical cases.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: all organisms examined so far are made of cells, and cells arise from pre-existing cells; cell theory successfully predicts the structure of newly discovered organisms. Arguments against: striated muscle fibres, aseptate fungal hyphae and giant algae such as Acetabularia do not fit the idea of a typical single-nucleus cell; viruses are not cellular yet show some properties of life. Supported judgement: Cell theory is robust as a general theory; apparent exceptions refine rather than overturn it, showing that scientific theories are generalisations that accommodate atypical cases.

items.stem: Compare light and electron microscopy and explain how each has contributed to our understanding of cell structure.
items.answer: Light: visible light, resolution ~200 nm, living specimens, colour stains, fluorescence, view cell divisions, nuclei, chloroplasts. Electron (TEM/SEM): electrons, resolution ~1 nm, dead specimens in vacuum, ultrastructure – membranes, ribosomes, mitochondrial cristae; freeze-fracture showed proteins spanning membranes; cryo-EM protein structure.
items.markingKey: Light: visible light, resolution ~200 nm, living specimens, colour stains, fluorescence, view cell divisions, nuclei, chloroplasts. Electron (TEM/SEM): electrons, resolution ~1 nm, dead specimens in vacuum, ultrastructure – membranes, ribosomes, mitochondrial cristae; freeze-fracture showed proteins spanning membranes; cryo-EM protein structure.

items.stem: Which observation is an exception, or a challenge, to the cell theory?
options: an onion epidermis cell with a cell wall
striated muscle fibres that contain many nuclei and are much longer than typical cells
a red blood cell of a frog containing a nucleus
a bacterium dividing by binary fission
items.answer: striated muscle fibres that contain many nuclei and are much longer than typical cells
items.markingKey: B. Muscle fibres challenge the idea of a cell as a single unit with one nucleus.

items.stem: Explain the difference between light microscopes and electron microscopes.
items.answer: Light microscopes use light, have resolution about 200 nm, can view living cells in colour; electron microscopes use electron beams, resolve down to about 0.1–1 nm, need dead specimens in a vacuum and give black-and-white images.
items.markingKey: Light microscopes use light, have resolution about 200 nm, can view living cells in colour; electron microscopes use electron beams, resolve down to about 0.1–1 nm, need dead specimens in a vacuum and give black-and-white images. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly describe the use of cryogenic electron microscopy to determine the structure of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein in 2020 and explain what it reveals about how developments in microscopy improve biological understanding.
items.answer: Within weeks, cryo-EM revealed the spike protein’s shape at near-atomic resolution. Rapid freezing preserves the native structure and the short electron wavelength gives very high resolution, supporting vaccine design.
items.markingKey: Context (Within weeks, cryo-EM revealed the spike protein’s shape at near-atomic resolution.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Rapid freezing preserves the native structure and the short electron wavelength gives very high resolution, supporting vaccine design. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how developments in microscopy improve biological understanding.

items.stem:
Mohammed measured six guard cells using an eyepiece graticule with the × 40 objective lens. A stage micrometer showed that at this magnification one eyepiece unit (epu) = 2.5 µm.

Cell | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6
Length / epu | 16 | 17 | 17 | 15 | 14 | 17

(a) Calculate the actual length of cell 1 in µm. [1]
(b) Calculate the mean length of the six cells. [2]
(c) Calculate the standard deviation of the cell lengths. [1]
(d) The diameter of the field of view is 500 µm. Estimate how many of the longest cells would fit across the field of view end to end. [1]
(e) Explain why the eyepiece graticule must be recalibrated when the objective lens is changed. [2]
(f) Suggest why a sample of at least six cells was measured. [2]
(g) Calculate the magnification of a drawing in which cell 1 is drawn 60 mm long. [2]
(h) Explain why a stage micrometer is needed to calibrate the eyepiece graticule. [2]
items.answer: (a) 40 µm (b) 40.0 µm (c) 3.2 µm (d) 11 (e) The graticule is in the eyepiece, so its divisions stay the same size while the specimen image is magnified by different amounts; the actual length represented by one epu changes. (f) Cells vary in size; a larger sample gives a more representative/reliable mean and allows variation (SD) to be estimated. (g) × 1500 (h) The stage micrometer has divisions of known size (10 µm), so the value of each eyepiece unit can be calculated at that magnification.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 16 × 2.5 = 40 µm (A1). (b) [2] Converts each to µm or mean epu × 2.5 (M1); 40.0 µm (A1). (c) [1] SD (n − 1) = 3.2 µm (A1); accept population SD 2.9. (d) [1] 500/42.5 = 11.8 → 11 whole cells (A1). (e) [2] Graticule scale fixed / specimen magnification changes (A1); epu value changes (A1). (f) [2] Biological variation (A1); reliable mean / representative (A1). (g) [2] 60 mm = 60 000 µm ÷ 40 µm (M1) = × 1500 (A1). (h) [2] Known scale (A1); calculation of eyepiece unit value (A1).

items.stem: Which structure is found in all prokaryotic cells?
items.answer: 70S ribosomes
items.markingKey: A. Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles but all have ribosomes.

items.stem: Distinguish between prokaryotic cells and eukaryotic cells.
items.answer: Prokaryotic cells lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, have naked circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and are usually 1–10 µm; eukaryotic cells have a nucleus containing linear DNA with histones, membrane-bound organelles, 80S ribosomes and are usually 10–100 µm.
items.markingKey: Prokaryotic cells lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, have naked circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and are usually 1–10 µm; eukaryotic cells have a nucleus containing linear DNA with histones, membrane-bound organelles, 80S ribosomes and are usually 10–100 µm. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain how the structure of a prokaryotic cell allows it to carry out all the functions of life.
items.answer: Plasma membrane controls exchange; cytoplasm contains enzymes for metabolism; 70S ribosomes synthesise proteins; naked circular DNA (and plasmids) carry genes for inheritance and control; cell wall protects against bursting; some have flagella for movement and pili for attachment or DNA transfer. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Plasma membrane controls exchange; cytoplasm contains enzymes for metabolism; 70S ribosomes synthesise proteins; naked circular DNA (and plasmids) carry genes for inheritance and control; cell wall protects against bursting; some have flagella for movement and pili for attachment or DNA transfer. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: An electron micrograph of a cell shows a nucleus, mitochondria and a large vacuole surrounded by a thick wall, but no chloroplasts. Suggest two possible cell types and how you would distinguish them.
items.answer: A plant root cell or a fungal cell; test the cell wall composition – cellulose (plant) or chitin (fungus); presence of starch grains or plastids suggests plant; hyphal arrangement suggests fungus.
items.markingKey: A plant root cell or a fungal cell; test the cell wall composition – cellulose (plant) or chitin (fungus); presence of starch grains or plastids suggests plant; hyphal arrangement suggests fungus.

items.stem: Briefly describe the bacterium Escherichia coli in the human gut and explain what it reveals about prokaryotic cell structure.
items.answer: E. coli is a rod about 2 µm long with a peptidoglycan wall, flagella, pili, a nucleoid and plasmids. It has all the functions of life without membrane-bound organelles: metabolism in the cytoplasm, protein synthesis on 70S ribosomes, DNA as a naked loop.
items.markingKey: Context (E. coli is a rod about 2 µm long with a peptidoglycan wall, flagella, pili, a nucleoid and plasmids.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It has all the functions of life without membrane-bound organelles: metabolism in the cytoplasm, protein synthesis on 70S ribosomes, DNA as a naked loop. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to prokaryotic cell structure.

items.stem: "Prokaryotic cells have no ribosomes because they have no organelles." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Prokaryotes do have ribosomes (70S); ribosomes are not membrane-bound, so they are present in all cells.
items.markingKey: Prokaryotes do have ribosomes (70S); ribosomes are not membrane-bound, so they are present in all cells. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Compare and contrast the structure of prokaryotic cells with that of plant and animal cells.
items.answer: Similarities: plasma membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, DNA. Differences: nucleus absent in prokaryotes; naked circular DNA vs linear with histones; 70S vs 80S; no membrane-bound organelles; peptidoglycan vs cellulose wall vs none; size 1–10 µm vs 10–100 µm; plants have chloroplasts and large vacuole, animals have centrioles; plasmids in prokaryotes.
items.markingKey: Similarities: plasma membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, DNA. Differences: nucleus absent in prokaryotes; naked circular DNA vs linear with histones; 70S vs 80S; no membrane-bound organelles; peptidoglycan vs cellulose wall vs none; size 1–10 µm vs 10–100 µm; plants have chloroplasts and large vacuole, animals have centrioles; plasmids in prokaryotes.

items.stem: "The distinction between prokaryotes and eukaryotes is the most fundamental division of living things." Discuss.
items.answer: The prokaryote–eukaryote distinction is a fundamental structural one, but molecular phylogeny shows the three-domain division better reflects evolutionary relationships.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the presence of a nucleus and compartmentalisation affects all aspects of cell biology; it is easily observed in electron micrographs. Arguments against: molecular evidence shows archaea are as different from bacteria as from eukaryotes, giving three domains; some features (e.g. 70S ribosomes in mitochondria) blur the boundary. Supported judgement: The prokaryote–eukaryote distinction is a fundamental structural one, but molecular phylogeny shows the three-domain division better reflects evolutionary relationships. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Why is compartmentalisation an advantage to eukaryotic cells?
options: It allows cells to be smaller.
It allows DNA to be circular.
Enzymes and substrates can be concentrated and incompatible reactions kept separate.
It removes the need for ribosomes.
items.answer: Enzymes and substrates can be concentrated and incompatible reactions kept separate.
items.markingKey: C. E.g. hydrolytic enzymes in lysosomes are kept away from the cytoplasm.

items.stem: Distinguish between fungal cells and plant cells.
items.answer: Fungal cells have walls of chitin, no chloroplasts and are heterotrophic, sometimes forming multinucleate hyphae; plant cells have cellulose walls, chloroplasts and are autotrophic.
items.markingKey: Fungal cells have walls of chitin, no chloroplasts and are heterotrophic, sometimes forming multinucleate hyphae; plant cells have cellulose walls, chloroplasts and are autotrophic. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Cells from the rough ER of pancreatic acinar cells are very abundant. What does this suggest about their function?
options: They synthesise large amounts of protein for secretion.
items.answer: They synthesise large amounts of protein for secretion.
items.markingKey: B. Digestive enzymes are made on ribosomes of rough ER and secreted.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "erythrocyte"?
options: A membrane derived from the host cell surrounding the capsid of some viruses, such as influenza and HIV
The smaller type of ribosome found in prokaryotes (and mitochondria and chloroplasts)
The last universal common ancestor, the most recent population of organisms from which all life on Earth descends
A red blood cell, which in mammals lacks a nucleus and mitochondria when mature
items.answer: A red blood cell, which in mammals lacks a nucleus and mitochondria when mature
items.markingKey: D. "erythrocyte" is a red blood cell, which in mammals lacks a nucleus and mitochondria when mature.

items.stem: Distinguish between mammalian red blood cells and phloem sieve tube elements.
items.answer: Both lack a nucleus when mature; red blood cells are free-floating, packed with haemoglobin and lack mitochondria, whereas sieve tube elements are joined end to end through sieve plates and are supported by companion cells that carry out metabolism for them.
items.markingKey: Both lack a nucleus when mature; red blood cells are free-floating, packed with haemoglobin and lack mitochondria, whereas sieve tube elements are joined end to end through sieve plates and are supported by companion cells that carry out metabolism for them. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Amara writes: "Mitochondria were made by the cell from its own membranes." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The endosymbiotic theory proposes they originated from free-living aerobic prokaryotes engulfed by an ancestral host cell.
items.markingKey: The endosymbiotic theory proposes they originated from free-living aerobic prokaryotes engulfed by an ancestral host cell. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Sequencing shows the genes in chloroplast DNA most closely resemble those of cyanobacteria. What conclusion is supported?
options: Chloroplasts descended from an engulfed cyanobacterium.
items.answer: Chloroplasts descended from an engulfed cyanobacterium.
items.markingKey: C. Molecular phylogeny places plastids within cyanobacteria.

items.stem: With reference to Paulinella chromatophora, an amoeba with a recently acquired cyanobacterial endosymbiont, explain how it illustrates endosymbiosis as an ongoing process.
items.answer: The amoeba contains photosynthetic “chromatophores” derived from a cyanobacterium about 100 million years ago. It shows a stage in which an engulfed prokaryote is becoming an organelle, as proposed for chloroplasts.
items.markingKey: Context (The amoeba contains photosynthetic “chromatophores” derived from a cyanobacterium about 100 million years ago.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It shows a stage in which an engulfed prokaryote is becoming an organelle, as proposed for chloroplasts. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to endosymbiosis as an ongoing process.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The endosymbiotic theory is now accepted as fact."
items.answer: Endosymbiosis is a well-supported theory accepted by biologists; calling it fact overstates certainty, but it is as strongly supported as any explanation in cell biology.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: many independent lines of evidence (DNA, ribosomes, membranes, division) support it; phylogenetic analysis places mitochondria within α-proteobacteria. Arguments against: the details of the host cell and sequence of events remain uncertain; scientific knowledge is always provisional. Supported judgement: Endosymbiosis is a well-supported theory accepted by biologists; calling it fact overstates certainty, but it is as strongly supported as any explanation in cell biology.

items.stem: Define the term "erythrocyte".
items.answer: A red blood cell, which in mammals lacks a nucleus and mitochondria when mature
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a red blood cell, which in mammals lacks a nucleus and mitochondria when mature. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Antibiotics such as chloramphenicol that inhibit 70S ribosomes can reduce protein synthesis in human mitochondria. What does this suggest?
options: Mitochondrial ribosomes resemble prokaryotic ribosomes, supporting endosymbiosis.
items.answer: Mitochondrial ribosomes resemble prokaryotic ribosomes, supporting endosymbiosis.
items.markingKey: A. Mitochondria share features with bacteria.

items.stem: Outline the endosymbiotic theory and evaluate the evidence for it.
items.answer: Host anaerobic cell engulfed aerobic prokaryote → mitochondrion, later photosynthetic prokaryote → chloroplast; not digested, mutualistic. Evidence: double membranes, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, binary fission, size, sequence similarity, antibiotic sensitivity. Evaluation: strong convergence; but many genes transferred to nucleus; cannot observe directly; Paulinella shows process.
items.markingKey: Host anaerobic cell engulfed aerobic prokaryote → mitochondrion, later photosynthetic prokaryote → chloroplast; not digested, mutualistic. Evidence: double membranes, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, binary fission, size, sequence similarity, antibiotic sensitivity. Evaluation: strong convergence; but many genes transferred to nucleus; cannot observe directly; Paulinella shows process.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "envelope".
items.answer: A membrane derived from the host cell surrounding the capsid of some viruses, such as influenza and HIV
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a membrane derived from the host cell surrounding the capsid of some viruses, such as influenza and HIV. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between non-enveloped viruses and enveloped viruses.
items.answer: Enveloped viruses (e.g. HIV, influenza) have an outer membrane derived from the host plasma membrane with viral glycoproteins; non-enveloped viruses (e.g. T4) have only a protein capsid.
items.markingKey: Enveloped viruses (e.g. HIV, influenza) have an outer membrane derived from the host plasma membrane with viral glycoproteins; non-enveloped viruses (e.g. T4) have only a protein capsid. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "A virus in the lysogenic cycle is inactive and harmless permanently." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A prophage can be induced to enter the lytic cycle, e.g. by UV or stress, killing the host and releasing virions.
items.markingKey: A prophage can be induced to enter the lytic cycle, e.g. by UV or stress, killing the host and releasing virions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using the T4 bacteriophage infecting Escherichia coli as an example, explain the lytic cycle.
items.answer: T4 attaches using tail fibres, injects DNA, and about 25 minutes later the cell bursts releasing 100–200 new phages. It shows how a virus redirects host machinery to make new virions and kills the host cell by lysis.
items.markingKey: Context (T4 attaches using tail fibres, injects DNA, and about 25 minutes later the cell bursts releasing 100–200 new phages.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It shows how a virus redirects host machinery to make new virions and kills the host cell by lysis. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the lytic cycle.

items.stem: A suspension of a phage isolated from sewage was diluted by a factor of 10⁷. 0.2 cm³ of the diluted suspension was spread with E. coli on an agar plate and 93 plaques formed. Calculate the concentration of infective phage particles in the original suspension, in plaque-forming units (pfu) per cm³.
items.answer: 4.65 × 10⁹ pfu cm⁻³
items.markingKey: pfu cm⁻³ = plaques ÷ (volume × dilution) = 93 ÷ (0.2 × 10⁻7) (M1) = 4.65 × 10⁹ (A1).

items.stem: Describe the structure of viruses and compare the lytic and lysogenic cycles of bacteriophages.
items.answer: Structure: nucleic acid (DNA or RNA), capsid of protein subunits, some enveloped, no cytoplasm or ribosomes, small (20–300 nm). Lytic: attach, inject, replicate, synthesise, assemble, lyse. Lysogenic: integrate prophage, replicated with host, induced to lytic. Comparison: both need host, attachment and injection similar; lytic kills quickly, lysogenic delays; λ vs T4.
items.markingKey: Structure: nucleic acid (DNA or RNA), capsid of protein subunits, some enveloped, no cytoplasm or ribosomes, small (20–300 nm). Lytic: attach, inject, replicate, synthesise, assemble, lyse. Lysogenic: integrate prophage, replicated with host, induced to lytic. Comparison: both need host, attachment and injection similar; lytic kills quickly, lysogenic delays; λ vs T4.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The DNA of a bacteriophage integrated into the bacterial chromosome during the lysogenic cycle"?
items.answer: prophage
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of prophage.

items.stem: A phage infects bacteria in a culture, but for several days no cells burst. When UV light is applied, many cells lyse. What is the best explanation?
options: The phage was destroyed by UV.
The phage was in the lysogenic cycle and UV triggered a switch to the lytic cycle.
items.answer: The phage was in the lysogenic cycle and UV triggered a switch to the lytic cycle.
items.markingKey: D. Stress such as UV can induce prophages.

items.stem: "Viruses should be classified as living organisms." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Viruses lie at the boundary of life; by the functions of life (metabolism, homeostasis, growth) they are not living, though they share evolution with living things.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they contain genetic material, evolve by natural selection and reproduce (inside hosts); giant viruses such as mimivirus have genes for some translation-related proteins. Arguments against: they have no metabolism, no cell structure and cannot reproduce independently; outside hosts they are inert particles that can even be crystallised. Supported judgement: Viruses lie at the boundary of life; by the functions of life (metabolism, homeostasis, growth) they are not living, though they share evolution with living things. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "magnification"?
options: A multinucleate cell or mass of cytoplasm formed by fusion of cells or by nuclear division without cell division, e.g. a striated muscle fibre
A membrane derived from the host cell surrounding the capsid of some viruses, such as influenza and HIV
How many times larger an image is than the actual object; magnification = image size ÷ actual size
The last universal common ancestor, the most recent population of organisms from which all life on Earth descends
items.answer: How many times larger an image is than the actual object; magnification = image size ÷ actual size
items.markingKey: C. "magnification" is how many times larger an image is than the actual object; magnification = image size ÷ actual size.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "prokaryote"?
options: An organism whose cell lacks a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; its DNA is a naked circular loop in the cytoplasm
The theory that all living organisms are composed of cells, the cell is the smallest unit of life, and cells only arise from pre-existing cells
The theory that mitochondria and chloroplasts evolved from free-living prokaryotes that were engulfed by a host cell and survived inside it
The protein coat of a virus, made of repeating subunits
items.answer: An organism whose cell lacks a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; its DNA is a naked circular loop in the cytoplasm
items.markingKey: A. "prokaryote" is an organism whose cell lacks a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; its DNA is a naked circular loop in the cytoplasm.

items.stem: Which condition is thought to have been absent from the atmosphere of the early Earth?
items.answer: free oxygen
items.markingKey: D. Oxygen accumulated only after photosynthesis evolved.

items.stem: Explain the evidence that mitochondria and chloroplasts evolved by endosymbiosis.
items.answer: They have a double membrane (inner from the prokaryote, outer from the host vesicle); their own naked circular DNA; 70S ribosomes; divide by binary fission; similar size to bacteria; their DNA sequences resemble those of α-proteobacteria and cyanobacteria respectively; antibiotics that affect bacteria affect them.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They have a double membrane (inner from the prokaryote, outer from the host vesicle); their own naked circular DNA; 70S ribosomes; divide by binary fission; similar size to bacteria; their DNA sequences resemble those of α-proteobacteria and cyanobacteria respectively; antibiotics that affect bacteria affect them. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the stages of the lytic cycle of a bacteriophage such as T4.
items.answer: Attachment to receptors on host cell; injection of viral DNA; host DNA degraded and host machinery used to replicate viral DNA and make capsid proteins; assembly of new virions; lysis of the cell by viral enzymes releases many phages.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Attachment to receptors on host cell; injection of viral DNA; host DNA degraded and host machinery used to replicate viral DNA and make capsid proteins; assembly of new virions; lysis of the cell by viral enzymes releases many phages. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain how the cell theory was developed using inductive reasoning.
items.answer: Many observations of different organisms (e.g. by Schleiden of plants and Schwann of animals) all showed cells; from these repeated observations a general theory that all organisms consist of cells was proposed, which is then tested by further observation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Many observations of different organisms (e.g. by Schleiden of plants and Schwann of animals) all showed cells; from these repeated observations a general theory that all organisms consist of cells was proposed, which is then tested by further observation. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: In an electron micrograph a cell shows a cell wall, ribosomes and a nucleoid, but no membrane-bound organelles. What is it?
items.answer: a prokaryote
items.markingKey: B. No nucleus or organelles = prokaryote.

items.stem: Distinguish between the hydrothermal vent hypothesis for the origin of life and the Miller–Urey hypothesis.
items.answer: Miller–Urey proposes organic molecules formed in a reducing atmosphere powered by lightning; the vent hypothesis proposes they formed in deep-sea vents using chemical energy from H₂ and mineral gradients.
items.markingKey: Miller–Urey proposes organic molecules formed in a reducing atmosphere powered by lightning; the vent hypothesis proposes they formed in deep-sea vents using chemical energy from H₂ and mineral gradients. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Mitochondria divide by a process similar to binary fission. How does this support the endosymbiotic theory?
options: Eukaryotic cells divide by binary fission.
It shows mitochondria are made by the nucleus.
Prokaryotes divide by binary fission, so mitochondria retain a prokaryotic mode of reproduction.
items.answer: Prokaryotes divide by binary fission, so mitochondria retain a prokaryotic mode of reproduction.
items.markingKey: D. New mitochondria arise only from existing ones.

items.stem: Briefly describe the T4 bacteriophage infecting Escherichia coli and explain what it reveals about the lytic cycle.
items.answer: T4 attaches using tail fibres, injects DNA, and about 25 minutes later the cell bursts releasing 100–200 new phages. It shows how a virus redirects host machinery to make new virions and kills the host cell by lysis.
items.markingKey: Context (T4 attaches using tail fibres, injects DNA, and about 25 minutes later the cell bursts releasing 100–200 new phages.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It shows how a virus redirects host machinery to make new virions and kills the host cell by lysis. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the lytic cycle.

items.stem: Freya writes: "Electron microscopes can be used to watch living cells divide." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Specimens for electron microscopy must be dead because they are fixed, stained and held in a vacuum.
items.markingKey: Specimens for electron microscopy must be dead because they are fixed, stained and held in a vacuum. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Bacterial cell walls are made of cellulose like plant cell walls." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Bacterial walls are made of peptidoglycan (murein); cellulose walls are found in plants.
items.markingKey: Bacterial walls are made of peptidoglycan (murein); cellulose walls are found in plants. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "The Miller–Urey experiment created living cells from gases." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It produced only simple organic molecules such as amino acids, not polymers or cells.
items.markingKey: It produced only simple organic molecules such as amino acids, not polymers or cells. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the work of Lynn Margulis in the 1960s shows the origin of eukaryotic cells by endosymbiosis.
items.answer: Margulis assembled evidence that mitochondria and chloroplasts originated as symbiotic bacteria, initially facing strong opposition. Her hypothesis was later strongly supported by DNA sequence data, showing how a paradigm shift occurs when evidence accumulates.
items.markingKey: Context (Margulis assembled evidence that mitochondria and chloroplasts originated as symbiotic bacteria, initially facing strong opposition.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Her hypothesis was later strongly supported by DNA sequence data, showing how a paradigm shift occurs when evidence accumulates. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the origin of eukaryotic cells by endosymbiosis.

items.stem: Viruses with RNA genomes and with DNA genomes, enveloped and non-enveloped, all infect cells. What does this diversity suggest about the origin of viruses?
options: Viruses may have arisen more than once (polyphyletic origin).
All viruses share one common ancestor.
items.answer: Viruses may have arisen more than once (polyphyletic origin).
items.markingKey: B. Structural diversity suggests multiple origins.

items.stem: An image of a cell is 45 mm long at × 1500 magnification. What is the actual length of the cell?
items.answer: 30 µm

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The distinction between prokaryotes and eukaryotes is the most fundamental division of living things."
items.answer: The prokaryote–eukaryote distinction is a fundamental structural one, but molecular phylogeny shows the three-domain division better reflects evolutionary relationships.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the presence of a nucleus and compartmentalisation affects all aspects of cell biology; it is easily observed in electron micrographs. Arguments against: molecular evidence shows archaea are as different from bacteria as from eukaryotes, giving three domains; some features (e.g. 70S ribosomes in mitochondria) blur the boundary. Supported judgement: The prokaryote–eukaryote distinction is a fundamental structural one, but molecular phylogeny shows the three-domain division better reflects evolutionary relationships.

items.stem: Outline the conditions on the early Earth and explain how experiments have tested hypotheses about the origin of the first cells.
items.answer: Conditions: reducing atmosphere (CH₄, NH₃, H₂, H₂O), no O₂, high UV, lightning, volcanic activity, high temperatures. Stages: monomers → polymers → self-replication → membranes. Miller–Urey produced amino acids; fatty-acid vesicles form spontaneously; ribozymes support RNA world; hydrothermal vent experiments; limitations – conditions uncertain, no cell produced.
items.markingKey: Conditions: reducing atmosphere (CH₄, NH₃, H₂, H₂O), no O₂, high UV, lightning, volcanic activity, high temperatures. Stages: monomers → polymers → self-replication → membranes. Miller–Urey produced amino acids; fatty-acid vesicles form spontaneously; ribozymes support RNA world; hydrothermal vent experiments; limitations – conditions uncertain, no cell produced.

items.stem: "The endosymbiotic theory is now accepted as fact." Discuss.
items.answer: Endosymbiosis is a well-supported theory accepted by biologists; calling it fact overstates certainty, but it is as strongly supported as any explanation in cell biology.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: many independent lines of evidence (DNA, ribosomes, membranes, division) support it; phylogenetic analysis places mitochondria within α-proteobacteria. Arguments against: the details of the host cell and sequence of events remain uncertain; scientific knowledge is always provisional. Supported judgement: Endosymbiosis is a well-supported theory accepted by biologists; calling it fact overstates certainty, but it is as strongly supported as any explanation in cell biology. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: "Viruses should be classified as living organisms." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Viruses lie at the boundary of life; by the functions of life (metabolism, homeostasis, growth) they are not living, though they share evolution with living things.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they contain genetic material, evolve by natural selection and reproduce (inside hosts); giant viruses such as mimivirus have genes for some translation-related proteins. Arguments against: they have no metabolism, no cell structure and cannot reproduce independently; outside hosts they are inert particles that can even be crystallised. Supported judgement: Viruses lie at the boundary of life; by the functions of life (metabolism, homeostasis, growth) they are not living, though they share evolution with living things. Markbands (8 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Electron microscopy of samples frozen rapidly in vitreous ice, allowing the structure of proteins to be determined at near-atomic resolution"?
items.answer: cryogenic electron microscopy
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of cryogenic electron microscopy.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "80S ribosome".
items.answer: The larger type of ribosome found in the cytoplasm and on the rough ER of eukaryotic cells
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the larger type of ribosome found in the cytoplasm and on the rough ER of eukaryotic cells. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "abiogenesis"?
options: The region of a prokaryotic cell where the circular DNA is located, not enclosed by a membrane
How many times larger an image is than the actual object; magnification = image size ÷ actual size
The origin of life from non-living matter through natural chemical processes
The division of a eukaryotic cell into membrane-bound organelles so that different processes can occur in separate, optimised environments
items.answer: The origin of life from non-living matter through natural chemical processes
items.markingKey: C. "abiogenesis" is the origin of life from non-living matter through natural chemical processes.

items.stem: A phloem sieve tube element is described as atypical because it
options: is dead at maturity like xylem
lacks a nucleus but is alive and depends on a companion cell
items.answer: lacks a nucleus but is alive and depends on a companion cell
items.markingKey: C. Sieve tube elements are living but enucleate.

items.stem: Why can the lysogenic cycle be advantageous to a phage?
options: It allows the phage to photosynthesise.
The viral genome is copied each time the host divides without killing it.
items.answer: The viral genome is copied each time the host divides without killing it.
items.markingKey: C. It spreads the virus vertically while host conditions are poor.

items.stem: Why is the magnification of a micrograph not a measure of how much detail is visible?
options: Magnification and resolution are the same thing.
Higher magnification always shows more detail.
Detail depends on resolution; enlarging beyond the resolution limit gives a blurred image.
Resolution depends only on the eyepiece.
items.answer: Detail depends on resolution; enlarging beyond the resolution limit gives a blurred image.
items.markingKey: C. Empty magnification adds no detail.

items.stem: Explain how electron micrographs can be used to identify the type of cell.
items.answer: Presence or absence of a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles distinguishes eukaryotes from prokaryotes; cell wall, chloroplasts and large vacuole indicate plant; chitin wall and no chloroplasts fungus; abundant particular organelles indicate function, e.g. many mitochondria in muscle.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Presence or absence of a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles distinguishes eukaryotes from prokaryotes; cell wall, chloroplasts and large vacuole indicate plant; chitin wall and no chloroplasts fungus; abundant particular organelles indicate function, e.g. many mitochondria in muscle. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between the hydrothermal vent hypothesis for the origin of life and the Miller–Urey hypothesis.
items.answer: Miller–Urey proposes organic molecules formed in a reducing atmosphere powered by lightning; the vent hypothesis proposes they formed in deep-sea vents using chemical energy from H₂ and mineral gradients.
items.markingKey: Miller–Urey proposes organic molecules formed in a reducing atmosphere powered by lightning; the vent hypothesis proposes they formed in deep-sea vents using chemical energy from H₂ and mineral gradients. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Mitochondria were made by the cell from its own membranes." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The endosymbiotic theory proposes they originated from free-living aerobic prokaryotes engulfed by an ancestral host cell.
items.markingKey: The endosymbiotic theory proposes they originated from free-living aerobic prokaryotes engulfed by an ancestral host cell. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Viruses are tiny bacteria." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Viruses are non-cellular: they lack cytoplasm, ribosomes and metabolism and can only reproduce inside host cells.
items.markingKey: Viruses are non-cellular: they lack cytoplasm, ribosomes and metabolism and can only reproduce inside host cells. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the use of cryogenic electron microscopy to determine the structure of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein in 2020 shows how developments in microscopy improve biological understanding.
items.answer: Within weeks, cryo-EM revealed the spike protein’s shape at near-atomic resolution. Rapid freezing preserves the native structure and the short electron wavelength gives very high resolution, supporting vaccine design.
items.markingKey: Context (Within weeks, cryo-EM revealed the spike protein’s shape at near-atomic resolution.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Rapid freezing preserves the native structure and the short electron wavelength gives very high resolution, supporting vaccine design. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how developments in microscopy improve biological understanding.

items.stem: With reference to pancreatic acinar cells that secrete digestive enzymes, explain how it illustrates the link between ultrastructure and function.
items.answer: Electron micrographs show extensive rough ER, many Golgi stacks and secretory vesicles. Abundant rough ER and Golgi reflect large-scale synthesis and processing of proteins for secretion.
items.markingKey: Context (Electron micrographs show extensive rough ER, many Golgi stacks and secretory vesicles.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Abundant rough ER and Golgi reflect large-scale synthesis and processing of proteins for secretion. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the link between ultrastructure and function.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Miller–Urey experiment (1953) shows how conditions on early Earth may have produced organic molecules.
items.answer: Electric sparks passed through methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water produced several amino acids within a week. It showed that, with an energy source and a reducing atmosphere, monomers needed for life form spontaneously.
items.markingKey: Context (Electric sparks passed through methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water produced several amino acids within a week.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It showed that, with an energy source and a reducing atmosphere, monomers needed for life form spontaneously. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how conditions on early Earth may have produced organic molecules.

items.stem: A suspension of a phage isolated from sewage was diluted by a factor of 10⁶. 0.1 cm³ of the diluted suspension was spread with E. coli on an agar plate and 148 plaques formed. Calculate the concentration of infective phage particles in the original suspension, in plaque-forming units (pfu) per cm³.
items.answer: 1.48 × 10⁹ pfu cm⁻³
items.markingKey: pfu cm⁻³ = plaques ÷ (volume × dilution) = 148 ÷ (0.1 × 10⁻6) (M1) = 1.48 × 10⁹ (A1).

items.stem: Ana writes: "To find the actual size of a cell, multiply the image size by the magnification." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification; both lengths must be in the same units.
items.markingKey: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification; both lengths must be in the same units. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Omar measured six onion epidermal cells using an eyepiece graticule with the × 10 objective lens. A stage micrometer showed that at this magnification one eyepiece unit (epu) = 10.0 µm.

Cell | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6
Length / epu | 19 | 27 | 23 | 20 | 29 | 28

(a) Calculate the actual length of cell 1 in µm. [1]
(b) Calculate the mean length of the six cells. [2]
(c) Calculate the standard deviation of the cell lengths. [1]
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 19 × 10.0 = 190 µm (A1). (b) [2] Converts each to µm or mean epu × 10.0 (M1); 243.3 µm (A1). (c) [1] SD (n − 1) = 42.7 µm (A1); accept population SD 39.0.

items.stem: "The origin of the first cells can be explained by testable scientific hypotheses." Discuss.
items.answer: Each stage is supported by experiments, but the whole process remains a hypothesis supported by indirect evidence; it is scientifically testable in parts but not fully explained.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: individual stages such as monomer synthesis (Miller–Urey) and vesicle formation have been reproduced in laboratories; ribozymes and genomic reconstruction of LUCA provide indirect evidence. Arguments against: the actual conditions of early Earth cannot be observed directly; no experiment has produced a living cell from non-living matter. Supported judgement: Each stage is supported by experiments, but the whole process remains a hypothesis supported by indirect evidence; it is scientifically testable in parts but not fully explained. items.stem:
Isabel measured six yeast cells using an eyepiece graticule with the × 100 objective lens. A stage micrometer showed that at this magnification one eyepiece unit (epu) = 1.0 µm.

Cell | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6
Length / epu | 7 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 4 | 6

(a) Calculate the actual length of cell 1 in µm. [1]
(b) Calculate the mean length of the six cells. [2]
(c) Calculate the standard deviation of the cell lengths. [1]
(d) The diameter of the field of view is 180 µm. Estimate how many of the longest cells would fit across the field of view end to end. [1]
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 7 × 1.0 = 7 µm (A1). (b) [2] Converts each to µm or mean epu × 1.0 (M1); 5.8 µm (A1). (c) [1] SD (n − 1) = 1.2 µm (A1); accept population SD 1.1. (d) [1] 180/7 = 25.7 → 25 whole cells (A1).

items.stem:
Omar measured six human cheek cells using an eyepiece graticule with the × 10 objective lens. A stage micrometer showed that at this magnification one eyepiece unit (epu) = 10.0 µm.

Cell | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6
Length / epu | 5 | 6 | 7 | 5 | 5 | 6

(a) Calculate the actual length of cell 1 in µm. [1]
(b) Calculate the mean length of the six cells. [2]
(c) Calculate the standard deviation of the cell lengths. [1]
(d) The diameter of the field of view is 1800 µm. Estimate how many of the longest cells would fit across the field of view end to end. [1]
(e) Explain why the eyepiece graticule must be recalibrated when the objective lens is changed. [2]
(f) Suggest why a sample of at least six cells was measured. [2]
(g) Calculate the magnification of a drawing in which cell 1 is drawn 60 mm long. [2]
(h) Explain why a stage micrometer is needed to calibrate the eyepiece graticule. [2]
items.answer: (a) 50 µm (b) 56.7 µm (c) 8.2 µm (d) 25 (e) The graticule is in the eyepiece, so its divisions stay the same size while the specimen image is magnified by different amounts; the actual length represented by one epu changes. (f) Cells vary in size; a larger sample gives a more representative/reliable mean and allows variation (SD) to be estimated. (g) × 1200 (h) The stage micrometer has divisions of known size (10 µm), so the value of each eyepiece unit can be calculated at that magnification.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 5 × 10.0 = 50 µm (A1). (b) [2] Converts each to µm or mean epu × 10.0 (M1); 56.7 µm (A1). (c) [1] SD (n − 1) = 8.2 µm (A1); accept population SD 7.5. (d) [1] 1800/70 = 25.7 → 25 whole cells (A1). (e) [2] Graticule scale fixed / specimen magnification changes (A1); epu value changes (A1). (f) [2] Biological variation (A1); reliable mean / representative (A1). (g) [2] 60 mm = 60 000 µm ÷ 50 µm (M1) = × 1200 (A1). (h) [2] Known scale (A1); calculation of eyepiece unit value (A1).
